title: Word Ladder
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing each word against every other word directly versus BFS generating letter variations on the fly.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given beginWord, endWord, and a wordList, a transformation sequence changes one letter at a time, with every intermediate word required to be in wordList. Return the length of the SHORTEST such transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord (counting all words in the sequence), or 0 if no such sequence exists.

blocks.text: Model every valid word as a node in an implicit graph, with an edge connecting two words whenever they differ by EXACTLY one letter. The shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord is then exactly the shortest path between these two nodes in this graph, found via standard BFS (since all edges have equal "weight" of one step).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Fewest Single-Letter Edits to Turn One Word Into Another, Only Passing Through Valid Dictionary Words
blocks.text: Picture a word game where each move changes exactly one letter, and every intermediate result must be a real dictionary word. Finding the fewest moves to go from a starting word to a target word is exactly a shortest-path search through a graph where dictionary words are connected whenever they differ by a single letter.

blocks.caption: Each word is a node; an edge connects words differing by one letter; the answer is the BFS shortest path

blocks.text: Result: 5 (the sequence hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog has 5 words).
Result: 0 ("cog" is not in the wordList, so it can never be reached).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If endWord is not even present in wordList, no valid transformation sequence can ever reach it, so the answer is immediately 0.

Observation 2: Since every "step" in a transformation sequence has equal cost (changing exactly one letter), a standard BFS (not a weighted shortest-path algorithm) correctly finds the shortest sequence length.

Observation 3: From the current word, generating EVERY possible one-letter variation (25 alternate letters at each of the word's positions) and checking each against a hash set of remaining valid words directly finds all "neighboring" words in the implicit graph, without ever needing to compare against every word in the list directly.

Observation 4: Removing a word from the set once it has been used as a BFS neighbor (visited) prevents revisiting it and keeps the search correctly bounded.
This leads to a standard BFS, generating letter variations directly at each step instead of comparing against every wordList entry.
For each word processed in the BFS, compare it directly against EVERY other remaining word in wordList to check if they differ by exactly one letter.
Why the code is written this way

items: Comparing directly against every remaining word finds valid neighbors clearly.

This costs O(word list size squared times word length) overall, since every word potentially compares against every other; directly generating letter variations reduces each word's neighbor search to O(word length times alphabet size).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(word list size squared times word length).
Space: O(word list size) for the set.
Limitation: generating every possible one-letter variation directly (25 alternatives per position) and checking each against a hash set in O(1) avoids comparing against every other word individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: If endWord is not in the word set, return 0 immediately. Otherwise, seed a BFS queue with beginWord, removing it from the set. Process the queue level by level (each level representing one additional transformation step): for the current word, if it equals endWord, return the current level. Otherwise, for every position in the word, try every one of the 25 OTHER possible letters, forming a candidate word; if that candidate is in the remaining word set, remove it (mark visited) and add it to the next level's queue. Increment the level after each round; if the queue empties without reaching endWord, return 0.
Use BFS, generating all possible one-letter variations at each position directly, checking each against a hash set in O(1).

Generating every possible one-letter variation directly (25 alternate letters at each position) and checking each against a hash set is equivalent to finding every valid neighbor in the implicit graph, but in O(word length times alphabet size) rather than comparing against every other word individually; removing a word from the set once used (marking it visited) ensures BFS never revisits it, and processing the queue level by level correctly finds the SHORTEST transformation sequence, since BFS guarantees the first time a target is reached is via the minimum number of steps.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(word list size times word length times alphabet size).
Space: O(word list size) for the set and queue.

blocks.text: Word Ladder is a classic "implicit graph" BFS problem: nodes and edges are never explicitly built, but generated on the fly via letter substitution.

items: Comparing each word against every other word in the list directly, instead of generating letter variations, causing unnecessary slowdown for large word lists.
Forgetting to remove used words from the set, allowing them to be revisited and potentially causing incorrect results or infinite loops.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "shortest sequence of one-letter-at-a-time word transformations", think: BFS over an implicit graph, generating letter variations directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The pairwise comparison approach costs O(word list size squared times length); the letter-generation BFS approach costs O(word list size times length times 26), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: BFS over an implicit graph, generating neighbors (letter variations) on the fly.
Core Idea: words are nodes, connected by an edge when differing by exactly one letter; the answer is the BFS shortest path length.
Time: O(word list size squared times length) for the brute force, O(word list size times length times 26) for the BFS approach.
Most Important Observation: generating letter variations directly avoids comparing against every other word explicitly.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, classic hard-tier implicit-graph BFS problem.
One line memory trick: BFS, generating letter swaps as neighbors.
